Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I feel on guard even inside my own home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
The world is a dangerous place
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is poorly integrated with the rest of the profile. The other threat items reflect hypervigilance and perceived danger (silence, being on guard at home), while memory and appraisal items center on intrusive, overwhelming captivity memories and beliefs that the world is dangerous or that she is 'going crazy.' Risk-taking points toward a different behavioral pattern that is not supported elsewhere, especially with Maladaptive Strategies absent and Threat not strongly linked outward in the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living
issues.explanation: 'Life Not Worth Living' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected appraisals, which otherwise focus on danger and loss of control ('world is dangerous,' 'going crazy'). It introduces a severe hopelessness/suicidal cognition not echoed in memory, threat, or strategy items. At PCL-5 53 severe symptoms are plausible, but this specific appraisal is insufficiently supported by the rest of the profile and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette:
Carmen, a sixty-six-year-old paramedic who had spent four decades responding to emergencies, was abducted three years ago while on a call to what turned out to be a staged address. The moment she stepped out of the ambulance, the unnatural quiet of the suburban street struck her—no birds, no traffic, no voices—and then two men grabbed her from behind and pulled her into a van. She was held captive for four days in a windowless room, bound and gagged, the only constant a deep, suffocating silence that stretched between her captors’ rare words. She eventually escaped when one of them left a door unlatched, but the memory of that stillness remained. It felt so extreme that even now she sometimes doubted it had happened to her—like a story she had been told rather than lived. Yet it forced its way into her mind without warning: while she was checking supplies in the ambulance bay, during dinner with her husband, in the middle of the night. When it came, the emotion was so overwhelming she had to stop whatever she was doing, pressing her palms against her thighs until the wave passed.

Those episodes began to frighten Carmen in a new way. Her reactions, she told herself, meant she was going crazy—a fear that took hold and would not let go. She became certain that the world was a dangerous place, that there was no safety anywhere, and that she could not stop bad things from happening to her. This conviction, in turn, seemed to pry the memory wide open. The more she believed she was losing her mind, the more the captivity scenes intruded, as if her own terror was the key that unlocked them. Each involuntary recall—the taste of the gag, the pressure of the ropes, the terrible silence—left her feeling jumpy and on edge. She began to notice that silence itself had become a trigger: at home, when the house fell quiet, her heart would race and she would freeze, certain something was about to happen. Even inside her own four walls, she felt perpetually on guard. She frequently looked behind her while walking from room to room, scanning for a follower she knew was not there. At work, she avoided quiet stretches of road and insisted on having the ambulance radio on at all times, rationalizing it as professional habit.

The memory’s power fed directly back into her negative appraisals. After each unbidden recollection, she felt more helpless than before—what could she possibly do to prevent danger when she could not even control her own mind? The world seemed even more treacherous, and her fear of going crazy deepened. She reduced her shifts, claiming she was tired, and began to withdraw from friends who called or visited. Her husband, Jorge, did not understand why she flinched when he entered a room silently, or why she searched every closet before they left the house. Carmen could not explain it; all she knew was that the cycle tightened with every passing month.

What finally brought her to seek help was a morning at the station when a prolonged silence in the dispatch room—no calls, no chatter—sent her into a full panic, and she collapsed behind the ambulance. Her supervisor urged her to see someone. Carmen agreed, but what frightened her most was the thought that she might truly be beyond repair. She hoped, against the weight of her certainty, that someone could show her a way out.
